**BalancedSubnet represents the current state-of-the-art method for mitigating memorization in language models through machine unlearning.**[1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02159v2)

Introduced in the ICLR 2025 paper "Mitigating Memorization in Language Models," it extends the Subnet approach by training a binary mask to identify and prune subnetworks responsible for memorized sequences while penalizing masks that affect non-memorized tasks.  This weight-based unlearning technique outperforms regularizers, fine-tuning, and other unlearning methods (e.g., Greedy, Durable, neuron-based like Hard Concrete) in reducing regurgitation while preserving downstream performance and ef
| % Memorized | % of artifact sequences (noise/backdoors) regurgitated verbatim via greedy decoding | Lower (ideally ~0%)  |
BalancedSubnet achieves near-complete memorization removal (0-0.06% memorized) with minimal degradation (e.g., 96.11-96.79% accuracy on math, perplexity 57.18-71.86 on language for 4-layer TinyMem).
It consistently excels across model sizes (2-16 layers), training durations, and data sizes, often reducing % memorized by ~100% with <5% performance drop.

## Best-fit shortlist

If you want the smallest set of public sources that best match the BalancedSubnet paper, use these three: **TinyMem synthetic sequences**, **Wikipedia-based toy language data**, and **The Pile / Pythia checkpoints**. That combination covers the paper’s main evaluation modes: controlled synthetic artifacts, natural-language memorization, and larger production-style models.[1](https://github.com/msakarvadia/memorization)

TinyMem injects artificial noise (±1 perturbations) or backdoors (trigger-replacement sequences), which simplifies detection but diverges from real memorization of PII, code, or copyrighted text in diverse corpora like The Pile.  Synthetic math/language tasks enable precise artifact control but may inflate unlearning efficacy, as real data lacks such clean "clean vs. memorized" splits; generalization to organic Pile-extracted sequences in Pythia is promising but limited to ~50-90% memorization r

BalancedSubnet extends Subnet unlearning by incorporating a balanced objective that penalizes masks affecting non-memorized tasks, addressing limitations in neuron- vs. weight-based methods from works like Chang et al. (2024) and Maini et al. (2023).
